messages.subject: Understanding aberrant fit index values
parts:
I'm using lavaan for the first time and have come across what looks like an aberrant fit index value in the summary obtained after fitting a CFA model. I'd like to better understand whether/why this is the case.

Some context: The data are not mine, but taken from OSF, and contain almost 40000 responses to 16 items intending to measure the "dark factor" of personality. I'm trying to run a CFA in which responses to all 16 items load on a single D-factor. Each response is given on a 5-point ordinal scale.

I've specified the model thus:
cfaFormula1 <- 'D =~ d1 + d2 + d3 + d4 + d5 + d6 + d7 + d8 +
d9 + d10 + d11 + d12 + d13 + d14 + d15 + d16'

And then am fitting it using the following command:
cfa1 <- cfa(cfaFormula1,
            data = mp,
            ordered = TRUE,
            estimator = "PML")

(Note that I specified the estimator as PML because I want to be able to compare models using BIC, and as far as I'm aware that is the only option for doing this with ordinal variables in lavaan---though as I say, I'm new to the package so please correct me if this is wrong.)

I then obtain a summary of the outcome thus:
summary(cfa1, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)

This gives me the following output (trimmed):
lavaan 0.6-19 ended normally after 67 iterations

  Estimator                                        PML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                        80

  Number of observations                         37744

Model Test User Model:
                                              Standard      Scaled
  Test Statistic                              8808.631   14493.473
  Degrees of freedom                               104     115.277
  P-value (Unknown)                                 NA       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                  0.608
    mean+var adjusted correction (PML)                            

Model Test Baseline Model:

  Test statistic                            537882.605   48902.728
  Degrees of freedom                               120      12.177
  P-value                                           NA       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                 10.999

User Model versus Baseline Model:

  Comparative Fit Index (CFI)                    0.984       0.706
  Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI)                       0.981       0.969

My confusion here lies in the CFI and TLI values listed in the "Scaled" column. As I understand it (from here), the CFI is calculated as (d(baseline) - d(user))/d(baseline), where d(x) = \chi^2(x) - df(x). From the scaled values provided in the output, I can manually calculate the scaled CFI as:

 ((48902 - 12) - (14493 - 115)) / (48902 - 12)
 ~ = .701
Given my rounding, this is basically consistent with the reported output.

If the TLI is calculated as (\chi^2(baseline)/df(baseline) - \chi^2(user)/df(user)) / (\chi^2(baseline)/df(baseline) - 1), then I get:

 (48902/12 - 14493/115) / (48902/12 - 1)
~ = .969
Given my rounding, this is again consistent with the reported output. So, both of the indices seem to be calculated correctly. Where I am confused is simply that the CFI is so much lower than the TLI, whereas everything I've read seems to suggest that the opposite should be true. The page I linked above does mention that the CFI will be too low if the RMSEA of the baseline model is less than .158, but when I run nullRMSEA(cfa1, scaled = TRUE) I get a value substantially higher than that (.345).

Can anyone help me shed some light on this, so I can better understand what's going on and why?

Thanks in advance.

messages.author: f6d12b388faad456
messages.subject: Re: Understanding aberrant fit index values
parts:
Hi, Peter,

TLI and CFI tend to have a very high correlation, but both can vary a lot depending on sample size, number and type of items, model type and so on. In a paper I am writing, my colleagues and I simulated more than 1.2 million datasets and the mean correlation between CFI and TLI was 0.851, but there were some some cases when the correlation was as low as 0.3.
I'm unaware about studies that focused on this specific correlation though.

Best,
Yago

messages.author: f6d12b388faad456
messages.subject: Re: Understanding aberrant fit index values
parts:
Hi, Peter.

Since this isn't our main question, I never thought much about that. While I was summarizing the data for the first time, I had the impression that the main source of discordance occurs when you fit more latent variables than exist in the population model. This leads to overfitting, with the CFI having an upper limit of 1, while TLI has no upper limit.

I tried to fit a lm, but due to the sample size, everything is statistically significant. Based on the effect sizes, I would say that the variables that really affect the correlation between CFI and TLI are:
 - Estimator (partial Eta²: 0.30 [0.26-0.33]): Compared to MLR, WLSMV lowers the correlation when `ordered = FALSE` (B: -0.185, SE: 0.017, t: -10.763, p < 2e-16), but not when `ordered = TRUE` (B: -0.024, SE: 0.018, t: -1.363, p = 0.173).
 - Fittel model (partial Eta²: 0.19 [0.15-0.22]): Compared to fitting a bifactor model, the correlation increases when fitting a unidimensional model (B: 0.216, SE: 0.019, t: 11.373, p < 2e-16) or a first-order bidimensional model (B: 0.195, SE: 0.019, t: 10.254, p  < 2e-16).
 - Population model (partial Eta²: 0.11 [0.08-0.14]): Compared to having a bifactor structure in the population, the correlation decreases when the structure is unidimensional model (B: -0.069, SE: 0.020, t: -3.444, p = 5.91e-4) or a first-order bidimensional structure (B: -0.049, SE: 0.020, t: -2.458, p  0.014).

Please, note that the aim of the study was not to explore the correlation between CFI and TLI, which is not even published yet, and these results are a shallow exploration I did after your question. So, I am not sure how generalizable they are.

Obs.: MLR cannot be used when `ordered = TRUE`. Thus, the estimator has three levels: MLR with `ordered = FALSE` (includes analysis with truly continuous items and with ordinal items treated as continuous), WLSMV with `ordered = FALSE` (same as before), and WLSMV with `ordered = TRUE` (only ordinal items)

Best,
Yago
